title: Uniform convergence under Dobrushin dependence
formal: For every \(a\in\)[0,1), does there exist a finite constant \(C_{a}\) such that the following holds uniformly? Let \(m\ge 1\), let H be a nonempty class of measurable binary functions on a measurable instance space X with finite VC dimension d, and let \(\mathrm{P}_{m}\) be a joint law of \(S=(Z_{1},\ldots ,Z_{m}), Z_{i}=(X_{i},Y_{i})\in X\times \{0,1\}\), whose marginals all equal D and whose total-variation Dobrushin coefficient is at most a. For every \(\delta \in (0,1)\), require \(\Pr _{S\sim \mathrm{P}_{m}}[\sup _{h\in H}|\mathrm{L}_{S}(h)- \mathrm{L}_{D}(h)|>C_{a}\sqrt{(d+\log (2/\delta ))/m}]\le \delta\). Here \(\mathrm{L}_{S}\) and \(\mathrm{L}_{D}\) are zero-one losses and the conditional-kernel and measurability conventions below are part of the model. This card reads the source’s proposed extension quantitatively, using the iid-order finite-VC rate stated in equation (18) of its full version; it is not merely a claim that some unspecified convergence rate exists.
context:
The paper proves learnability for finite-VC classes under the ordinary total-variation Dobrushin condition. A guarantee for the hypothesis returned by that learner does not assert that every hypothesis has an accurate empirical loss.

Theorem 5.3 assumes \(\alpha _{\mathrm{log}}<1/2\), where \(\alpha _{\mathrm{log}}\) sums worst-case logarithmic probability-ratio influences. Ordinary total-variation influences are no larger, so this is a stronger restriction. The resulting finite-VC sample complexity is \(O((d+\log (1/\delta ))/\varepsilon ^{2})\) at fixed slack, as stated in equation (18).

The source separately gives a Gaussian-complexity theorem for much more general real-valued losses. This card retains its explicit finite-VC classification question and asks for the same rate with ordinary Dobrushin dependence. It does not demand the full real-valued empirical-process theorem.

The question allows its constant to depend on \(a<1\). It asks whether the usual sample-size dependence survives throughout that regime, without specifying an optimal blow-up as a approaches the boundary.
why: Would determine whether the standard weak-influence condition suffices for the uniform statistical guarantees that make finite VC dimension useful, beyond the already-known existence of a successful learner.
status_note: Read the source definitions, its learning theorem and the stronger uniform-convergence theorem in the conference and full versions. Searches through 12 September 2026 did not locate a proof or refutation of the displayed ordinary-Dobrushin finite-VC rate. The 2026 product-space uniform-law paper concerns another estimator and distributional structure, not this empirical-mean extension. The lack of a located resolution is not an exhaustive current-status guarantee.

importance.reason: A structural boundary for transferring VC uniform-convergence guarantees from independent samples to dependent data, with implications for empirical-risk validation. Existing score retained.

sentences: A dependent training sample has identical marginal distributions and a bounded total influence on every coordinate.
Uniform convergence requires every hypothesis’s empirical zero-one loss to approximate its population loss.
The card asks whether every finite-VC class has the usual square-root rate when the ordinary Dobrushin coefficient stays below one.
The source already proves learnability under that condition, but its uniform-convergence theorem requires stronger logarithmic influences.
The formulation makes the iid-order rate and fixed dependence slack explicit, without claiming an optimal constant near the boundary.

A finite \(F\subseteq X\) is shattered if every binary labeling of F is the restriction of a member of H. \(\operatorname{VC}(H)\) is the largest size of a shattered set, or infinity if these sizes are unbounded. The hypothesis \(d<\infty\) includes \(d=0\). The constant \(C_{a}\) may depend on the fixed upper bound a and may diverge as a approaches one, but must be independent of \(m,d,\delta ,X,H,D\) and \(\mathrm{P}_{m}\). The law \(\mathrm{P}_{m}\) may be different for each m; no consistency of an infinite process is required. The logarithm is natural. This is a statistical inequality, with no algorithmic running-time requirement.
answer_criterion: Prove existence of such a constant for every fixed \(a<1\), uniformly over all the displayed models and parameters, or refute this quantified rate. A negative answer must defeat every proposed constant for some fixed \(a<1; a\) family with its coefficient tending to one does not by itself suffice. Proving generalization only for a particular learner, a bound depending on the cardinality of H, a slower rate, or a result needing stronger log-influence assumptions does not establish the displayed extension.
